source.title: Jo-SRC: A Contrastive Approach for Combating Noisy Labels
source.authors: Ya-Zhou Yao; Ze-Ren Sun; Chuan-Yi Zhang; Fu-Min Shen; Qi Wu; Jian Zhang; Zhen-Min Tang

record.tranche_reason: The study reports training dynamics for clean and noisy examples under synthetic label corruption, using prediction accuracy rather than the original studies’ random-label fitting setup.
record.gate_note: The study does not test completely random labels, unstructured inputs, fit time, smooth test-error degradation across corruption rates, or whether explicit regularizers are necessary or sufficient. Figure 5 reports training prediction accuracy for sample groups; the text describes trends and comparisons but gives no numeric values for those curves. Other noisy-label benchmark accuracies are not rows because they do not measure a behavior named by these claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study uses the clean-patterns-first claim to motivate noisy-label mitigation. Its own results compare mitigation methods, including training-sample prediction accuracy, but do not establish that clean patterns are learned before noisy labels. Figure 5's reported trends and rankings do not measure that temporal ordering.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that Jo-SRC improves classification performance on synthetic and real-world noisy-label datasets, with ablations supporting its sample selection, treatment of noisy samples, and consistency regularization.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses synthetic and real-world noisy-label benchmarks, sample selection, mean-teacher relabeling, and consistency regularization; it does not reproduce random-label fitting.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported training-dynamics result is for CIFAR80N-O with Symmetry-20%; the text does not report corresponding Figure 5 dynamics for other corruption settings.

fits_no_version.finding: Clean-sample prediction accuracy increases during training across the Figure 5 mitigation methods.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The evaluated noisy-label mitigation methods learn clean training samples during training.

fits_no_version.finding: JoCoR and Jo-SRC have the lowest prediction accuracy against the given noisy labels.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Some sample-selection and regularization methods suppress fitting of corrupted labels more effectively than competing mitigation methods.

fits_no_version.finding: Jo-SRC achieves the highest accuracy against the true labels of ID noisy samples.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Jo-SRC recovers underlying class information from mislabeled in-distribution samples better than the compared methods.

record.problems: The relevant training-dynamics evidence is presented in Figure 5 without numeric values in the text. The reported dynamics use a single synthetic corruption setting, and the study does not test completely random labels.
record.rows_left_out: No additional Figure 5 rows retained: the text reports only the aggregate comparisons captured in R1–R3, while individual curve values are figure-only. Benchmark test-accuracy tables concern noisy-label method performance rather than the specified claim versions.

untested.parts: Near-zero training error on completely random labels, chance test performance, and unchanged architecture and training hyperparameters.
Relative time to fit true versus random labels and convergence slowing with increasing corruption.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, and Gaussian-noise inputs.

Perfect training fit together with steadily increasing test error across corruption levels from none to all. The benchmark tables report test accuracy at selected noise rates without establishing the claimed training fit.
Whether weight decay, dropout, and augmentation prevent random-label fitting, and whether removing them impairs true-label generalization.

The temporal ordering of learning shared real-data patterns before memorizing noisy labels. The study cites this ordering as motivation but does not establish it through its reported method comparisons.

record.verdict_notes: Remove both proposed V6 verdicts. A mitigation method's suppression of memorization does not challenge the claimed natural learning order, and failure to test that order is an untested part rather than a scope limitation. Numerical Figure 5 trajectories cannot be recovered from the supplied text.

versions.untested_parts: Completely random labels, training error, chance test error, unchanged architecture and hyperparameters.
Relative training time and convergence rate as label corruption increases.
Shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, and Gaussian-noise inputs.
Perfect training fit and test error across the full range of random-label corruption.
Whether weight decay, dropout, or data augmentation stop random-label fitting or affect true-label generalization when removed.
The study examines synthetic noisy labels, not completely random labels, and does not directly establish that networks first learn shared real-data patterns and later memorize noise.

rows.subject: 7-layer DNN
rows.operation_detail: Tracked prediction accuracy on clean CIFAR80N-O training samples during training.
rows.value: figure only; text says all methods achieve increasing prediction accuracy on clean samples
rows.note: Text describes the trend across methods; the figure supplies the curves without tabulated values.
rows.check: Increasing clean-sample accuracy alone does not establish V6's learning order. This row aggregates mitigation methods rather than recording a claim-testing comparison. Symmetry-20% denotes corruption within the in-distribution subset; the overall noise ratio is 36%.

rows.subject: 7-layer DNN
rows.operation_detail: Tracked prediction accuracy on noisy samples against their given labels during training.
rows.value: figure only; text says JoCoR and Jo-SRC achieve the lowest prediction accuracy on noisy samples
rows.note: The text reports a relative comparison, not a numeric fitting rate or a direct test of completely random labels.
rows.check: Lower accuracy against noisy labels measures mitigation effectiveness, not whether clean patterns precede noise memorization. Split ID and OOD samples into separate rows if retaining these method-performance results. The overall noise ratio is 36%.

rows.subject: 7-layer DNN
rows.operation_detail: Tracked prediction accuracy on ID noisy samples against their true labels during training.
rows.value: figure only; text says Jo-SRC achieves the best prediction accuracy on ID noisy samples w.r.t. their true labels
rows.note: This is a relative comparison; the plot values are not reported numerically in the text.
rows.check: Jo-SRC's superior recovery of true labels measures mitigation effectiveness and does not establish V6's temporal ordering. Its partial state is unsupported as a verdict on V6. The overall noise ratio is 36%.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
